translations.text: The author of this work is Bede, a wise noble priest, a man of the grace of God in wisdom and in piety.
Bede found, moreover, a helper, namely Albinus, the most venerable abbot,
the man who was trained [?] in all disciplines by those learned men, Bishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian.
For Albinus learned from the disciples of Gregory the things that were done in the province of the people of Kent (Cantuarii) and in the
neighbouring territories, and what he found in the old histories of writing or in the tradition of the elders; and Albinus conveyed to Bede the
things that Nothelm, a noble priest of the church of London, had related to him, whether from letters or from conversations.
It was Nothelm who brought a letter from Gregory [?] from Rome to the Saxons.
It is these that Albinus directed to be aids [?] for the work [?] of holy Bede.
From the beginning of the history up to the faith of the Saxons, moreover, Bede learned and gathered it from the writings of the ancients, from here and there.
Daniel, moreover, bishop of the West Saxons, sent to them by letters the history of his own people, and of the South Saxons, and of the Isle of Wight.

The beginning of the faith of the Mercian Saxons, moreover, he learned — how it came about through the two noble priests Cedd and Chad, and how through them the faith of the East Saxons was renewed — namely
from the brothers of the monastery that was built by them, namely Lastingham.
Of the things that were done in the province of the East Saxons, he obtained part from the traditions of the ancients and another part from the account of Abbot Esi.
The things, moreover, that were done with regard to the faith of Christ in the province of Lindsey he learned from the living voice of the noble priest Cyneberht.
As for the traditions of the Northumbrians, that is, the old histories of the northern Saxons, he found many of them and brought them in himself.
Britain, an island of the ocean, which was once called Albion, is eight hundred thousand paces in length, two hundred
in breadth; its circumference, moreover, that is, seventy-five miles multiplied by forty-eight [?]...
Romanus, the chief [?] of the church of Rochester, was drowned in the Italian sea. It was to that church that Paulinus assigned the pallium which he brought from Honorius.
James, moreover, the deacon of Paulinus, an ecclesiastical man and a holy man and a master of chanting, was in Cair [?] for a long time.
